hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Signed Store app; only child is WerFault.
Dropped in Temp, launched on NASHUA by PSEXESVC after PsExec with cleartext password; spawned the harvesting PowerShell.
Password-protected the harvested working.zip, then was wiped with sdelete64.
Anti-forensic wiping of Rar.exe, working.zip, the .scr dropper and Draft.Zip.
Azure guest log collector; lsass handle 0x10 only.
Run by pbeesly's PowerShell as part of the LSASS credential-access toolchain.
Used with cleartext domain password to run python.exe on NASHUA.
Anti-forensic wiping of dropper and staged archives on SCRANTON.
Dropper executed by explorer as pbeesly with /S, spawning cmd.exe.
Compiled attacker C# DLLs from temp cmdline files under hidden PowerShell.
Unsigned non-Microsoft binary in System32 launched elevated via -verb runas.
Three launches by cmd.exe just before compilation and .lnk writes; known UAC-bypass binary.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Evidence of credential dumping or theft on Windows hosts, such as LSASS memory access by non-standard processes, use of known dumping tools (e.g., Mimikatz, ProcDump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump), SAM/NTDS.dit or registry hive extraction, DPAPI secret access, or anomalous authentication with stolen credentials.
frame.what_would_refute: No evidence of credential-dumping tooling or LSASS/hive access on Windows hosts, and no anomalous use of harvested credentials, with credential access activity attributable only to sanctioned administrative or security tooling.

verdict.rationale: 6 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I01 T1003.001 (F01, F10, F17, F31, F48, F53, F63, F64), I03 T1187 (F21), I05 T1552.001 (F03, F59), I06 T1552.001 (F28, F61), I07 T1552.001 (F60), I08 T1552.004 (F27, F57)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: pbeesly's PowerShell on scranton and nashua harvested credential-named files (*pass*, *login*, *vpn, *psw*) and archived them, alongside Sysinternals download, shellcode/PE in-memory loaders and a hidden encoded command — attacker credential-access tooling, though not an OS store dump.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Extra 0x1000 LSASS handle by PowerShell on SCRANTON; full-access handles already anchored.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: No SAM hive object access, no reg save/esentutl/ntdsutil command lines in Sysmon or Security process creation.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit access or ntdsutil/vssadmin; Zeek drsuapi traffic is only Bind/CrackNames/Unbind with no DsGetNCChanges.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: All LSA secret reads are LOCAL SERVICE querying Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC (AccessMask 0x2) on nashua/scranton/utica — routine OS machine-account access.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No object access to any Cache registry path or SECURITY\Cache hive.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: One 4662 on newyork.dmevals.local shows DS-Replication-Get-Changes (1131f6aa) access, but by the host's own machine account NEWYORK$ on itself and only once; no DsGetNCChanges in Zeek and no dcsync/lsadump strings, so DCSync is unconfirmed.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture behaviour observed is a bounded netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' pair on scranton.dmevals.local, both spawned by the Microsoft-signed (win.Company 'Microsoft CoreXT') Azure Network Watcher agent service started by services.exe, with adjacent logman ETL traces from WaAppAgent.exe. No Npcap/WinPcap driver load, no pcap/tshark/dumpcap/windump/rawcap command lines, no capture-related service installs (7045 = PSEXESVC x4, Java VM Support Service), and no sniffing/promiscuous service in zeek. The lone rare zeek port 1234 session is ordinary application traffic to a peer that also serves 443.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: .scr dropper executed by pbeesly on SCRANTON (anchor).

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No hook/keylog DLL loads, no GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx script blocks, no keyboard-layout persistence or keylogger service; only benign Preload and WindowsDefender Run writes.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: All credential/prompt/consent matches were Microsoft consent.exe UAC prompts launched by SYSTEM; no fake credential dialogs from user-writable paths.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No wwwroot/inetpub file writes, no IIS/appcmd activity, no object access to web roots and no login/portal HTTP traffic in Zeek.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: powershell.exe PID 2976 (running a VirtualAlloc/CreateThread shellcode loader) created a remote thread inside lsass.exe on scranton, and a second powershell opened 0x1000 handles to lsass/winlogon while enumerating token privileges.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No failed-logon events (4625/4771/4776/4648) in windows.security or windows.other; the 218 LogonType 3 successes are machine-account (NEWYORK$) logons from loopback/IPv6/10.0.0.4 with no failure burst.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: Only runas-related hit is a local UAC elevation of hostui.exe by pbeesly on scranton; no repeated credential attempts and no 4625 failures to support guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: Credential material was harvested on scranton (PowerShell.exe as SYSTEM opening lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff, wsmprovhost.exe opening lsass on nashua, Get-PrivateKeys exporting .pfx with hardcoded password, hardcoded PSCredential in Invoke-Exfil), but no cracking tooling (hashcat/john/Mimikatz/reg save/ntdsutil/vssadmin/esentutl) and SAM handles only from lsass.exe.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: All spraying checks (4625 by user, by source IP, 1-minute interval, windows.other) returned zero hits; only successful logons present.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No 4625 by TargetUserName/IpAddress and no curl/Invoke-WebRequest/wget process creations; the only PSCredential use is a single hardcoded account for WebDAV exfiltration staging.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA interception artifacts in any dataset. SmartCard/Crypto/Credential registry hits were all Sysmon event.code 12 reads (SmartCardRoot certificate store accessed by powershell.exe, consent.exe, wmiprvse.exe, lsass.exe, rundll32.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe) or normal boot-time value sets by smss.exe/lsass.exe/services.exe/taskhostw.exe. Zero script blocks referenced SmartCard, MFA, Telephony/TAPI, RADIUS/NPS, OTP, CredentialProvider, Winlogon, netsh or proxy. The only token-related process was the standard svchost.exe TokenBroker service. 4648 events were PsExec (PSEXESVC.exe) explicit-credential logons for pbeesly and routine DWM-/UMFD-/machine-account logons; the two LogonType 10 RDP logons used Negotiate/User32, not a smart-card or MFA provider. The PowerShell 'Credential' hit was Invoke-Exfil exfiltration tooling, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: WebDAV share mapped with hardcoded creds for exfil (anchor).

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local the pbeesly PowerShell stager (PID 2976, hidden -ep bypass, shellcode decoded from monkey.png and run via VirtualAlloc/CreateThread) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff and UNKNOWN call traces at 03:05:16Z, consistent with in-memory credential access via exploitation/injection rather than a named dumping tool. No 4688/4104 lsass/comsvcs/MiniDump command lines exist, and the bulk of LSASS handles come from legitimate svchost/AV/telemetry/OS components, so the technique is assessed suspicious rather than confirmed malicious.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser cookie/session store was read, copied or replayed. The 162 sysmon file-create hits were svchost.exe writing EventLog lastalive*.dat files; the single INetCookies event was the WARP JIT service's own LocalService container created by svchost.exe (SYSTEM). No sysmon process-access/file-create touched Chrome/Firefox/Edge Cookies, Login Data, Web Data or Local State, no browser process appears in sysmon process creation, the 4688 hits were SearchProtocolHost.exe, the 4104 hits were built-in module manifests plus pbeesly's screenshot/7-Zip/WebDAV exfil functions, and zeek HTTP was WebDAV upload of OfficeSupplies.7z rather than cookie replay.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Unsecured credentials harvested: hardcoded passwords in scripts (saribas, lolol, MyCozyPassw0rd!, Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) and certificate exports staged/exfiltrated.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Credential-named file harvesting plus password-protected RAR on NASHUA and cleartext passwords in PsExec and Invoke-Exfil.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: Registry credential-key writes were all by legitimate system processes (svchost, winlogon, lsass, services); no attacker credential reads.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history, Get-History or history file access in any dataset.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certs to .pfx on SCRANTON (anchor).

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL/GPT file writes were routine Group Policy client (svchost.exe) DataStore caching; no Groups.xml/cpassword access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local an interactive pbeesly PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16 with UNKNOWN-module call traces, immediately after running accesschk.exe and amid sdelete wiping and Invoke-Exfil staging — consistent with LSASS memory credential access, though no dump file or credential artifact was captured. Other LSASS handles (svchost, wininit, csrss, AV/telemetry, wsmprovhost Get-Process -IncludeUserName) are benign.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No access to browser credential stores (Login Data, Cookies, Local State, logins.json) in process creation, file creation, 4663, PowerShell or other-channel logs; the single INetCookies write was a LocalService svchost artifact.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: Unsigned hostui.exe launched elevated from PowerShell on SCRANTON.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/LastPass/Bitwarden references in any dataset; only attacker 7-Zip staging of the Downloads folder was seen.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Hidden, EP-bypassed PowerShell (PID 2976, parent control.exe) decoded a steganographic payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png, compiled code via csc.exe from Temp\qkbkqqbs, and opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16Z.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: All lsass.exe/cryptdll.dll module loads are Microsoft-signed System32 DLLs; no 5136/4739 directory or policy changes; wsmprovhost LSASS access has a PowerShell-cmdlet call trace.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No writes to LSA Notification Packages or Password Filter values and no new DLLs in System32/SysWOW64; only LsaCfgFlagsDefault/LsaPid/ProductType writes.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: The only matching 4104 script block is the stock Microsoft xActiveDirectory DSC module MSFT_xADCommon.ps1 run as SYSTEM; no 4739 events or reversible-encryption commands.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/4738/5136 events; 4670 hits are routine token DACL changes by SearchIndexer/svchost/services on machine accounts.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: cloudAP/aadcloudap/MicrosoftAccountCloudAP/ngc DLL loads are Microsoft-signed Windows Hello/Azure AD join components; no cloudap/azuread file creation or directory changes.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No network-provider or credential-provider DLL registration, registry writes, or dropped provider DLLs in the retrieved data.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No interception/relay evidence. The 4663/4656 hits are pbeesly's own PowerShell/cmd access to LSA/Winlogon registry keys on scranton (local credential access), and 4624s on newyork are machine-account type-3 logons. The actual intrusion used direct PsExec with a plaintext password and a python payload, not AiTM.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: Zeek shows only routine DNS/NBNS lookups (wpad NXDOMAIN, SCRANTON/NASHUA NB broadcasts) and SMB mapping to the DC 10.0.0.4; no rogue responder or relayed authentication. PSEXESVC service installs on nashua are the attacker's own PsExec execution, not relay artifacts.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Only read-only 'arp.exe /a' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by Azure GuestAgent/Telemetry/WaAppAgent alongside ipconfig/route/netsh trace — standard Azure VM diagnostics. No ARP cache modification or poisoning tooling.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: Zero hits for DHCP client/server events (1341/1342/1020/1063) and no UDP 5156/5157 anomalies; only normal broadcast NBNS/NetBIOS traffic and read-only ipconfig /all by Azure agents.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Hidden PowerShell implant on scranton.dmevals.local (PID 2976, parent control.exe, steganographic monkey.png payload) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29, inside a staged toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-SeaDukeStage).

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: LSASS access that could yield krbtgt material is present, but no forged-TGT indicators: all 4768 are pre-authenticated (PreAuthType 2) AES256 requests for pbeesly/SCRANTON$, no anomalous privileged logons or 4672 target users.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 4769 requests are for machine accounts and krbtgt with AES256 and status 0x0; no service-account tickets or forged-ticket logon anomalies observed.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 (0x17) TGS requests, no service-account SPN ticket burst, and no Kerberoasting tooling in process creation or PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All AS-REQs show PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication performed) and no Rubeus/GetNPUsers/ASREP activity was found in Sysmon or PowerShell telemetry.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts: no SAML/cookie/token-forgery script blocks, no anomalous LogonProcessName, no SSO/ADFS endpoints. Credential-access precursor (PowerShell->LSASS 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton, cert private-key export by pbeesly) is present but is not web-credential forgery.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: 4663 cookie-file check returned zero hits; no cookie/session-token handling in PowerShell; Zeek window (non-overlapping) shows only internal DNS/TLS/HTTP to 192.168.0.4.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Logons are normal Kerberos/Advapi machine and SYSTEM accounts plus pbeesly NTLM/RDP and PsExec 4648 to NASHUA; no SAML/ADFS/AADSSO artifacts in any retrieved event.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/authenticator/OTP/verification-prompt generation artifacts in any dataset: sysmon process-creation sweep for mfa/auth/otp/token/push/login/azure/dsregcmd returned only benign Azure guest-agent and OS components (dsregcmd.exe under svchost -s Schedule, TokenBroker/PushToInstall services, CollectGuestLogs, logman, NetworkWatcherAgent); windows.other message sweep for mfa/multi-factor/authenticator/one-time/verification code/phonefactor returned 0 rows; no 4625 failed-logon burst (C318/C319 zero hits) and only one 4776 (pbeesly from 10.0.1.4), so no prompt-bombing pattern. The window's real activity is credential access/lateral movement (PsExec64 with plaintext dmevals\pbeesly password to NASHUA, 4648 explicit-credential logons) and collection (recursive file harvesting into working.zip, Rar staging, sdelete64 cleanup) - not T1621.

args.query: event.code:1

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot rare credential-dumping tooling (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs, rundll32, reg save, ntdsutil, vssadmin) among the 447 process-create events.

args.query: event.code:10

checks.purpose: Stack process-access GrantedAccess values to find LSASS-targeting access masks (0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1fffff) among the 39283 access events.

args.query: event.code:4663

checks.purpose: Stack object names on object-access events to find SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive or lsass handles being read.

args.query: event.code:4688

checks.purpose: Stack process-creation executables to spot dumping utilities or reg.exe/ntdsutil/vssadmin invocations.

args.query: FROM windows.powershell METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*mimikatz*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*lsass*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*minidump*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*sekurlsa*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ScriptBlockText) LIKE "*ntds*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*comsvcs*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, win.ScriptBlockText, process.command_line, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Search PowerShell script blocks and command lines for credential-dumping keywords.

args.query: FROM windows.other METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*lsass*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*sam*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*ntds*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*minidump*" OR TO_LOWER(process.executable) LIKE "*dump*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, event.code, message, process.executable, _id, _index

findings.title: Credential-harvesting PowerShell on scranton/nashua (file collection of *pass*/*login*/*vpn*, Sysinternals download, hidden encoded loader)
findings.summary: Under user pbeesly, PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local (02:56:17Z) and nashua.dmevals.local (03:15:59Z) enumerated the user profile for *.doc/*.xls/*.pdf/*.pst plus *psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *sifr*, *sifer*, *vpn* files and compressed them with Compress-Archive — credential harvesting from disk. On scranton the same session expanded SysinternalsSuite.zip into Downloads, created HKCU\Software\Classes\Folder\shell\open command keys, ran a VirtualAlloc/CreateThread shellcode loader, a GetProcAddress/ReflectedDelegate base64 PE loader, and a 'powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e' encoded command (03:21:28Z). This is attacker tooling on the host, but it is file-based credential collection and in-memory execution, not an OS credential-store dump: no SAM/SECURITY hive read (0 hits for 4663 ObjectName *SAM*/*SECURITY*/*Cache*), no reg save/ntdsutil/vssadmin/procdump/comsvcs command lines, and no dump artefacts were found.

findings.title: WebDAV forced-authentication (DavClnt / WebDAV-MiniRedir) from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4
findings.summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:18 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (the same address that appears as SCRANTON$ / scranton.dmevals.local in the Windows datasets) issued 36 WebDAV-style HTTP requests to 192.168.0.4:80 — 10 OPTIONS and 26 PROPFIND — with user agents 'DavClnt' and 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362', targeting /webdav and /webdav/. The sequence shows the classic forced-authentication handshake: an initial OPTIONS / with DavClnt returned 403, then OPTIONS /webdav returned 401 Unauthorized, a 301 redirect, OPTIONS /webdav/ returned 401 then 200, and PROPFIND /webdav/ returned 401 then 207 Multi-Status. The 401 challenges followed by successful 200/207 responses indicate the client was induced to present credentials to an attacker-controlled WebDAV endpoint, which is exactly the T1187 credential-capture pattern. This is not normal browsing: the destination 192.168.0.4 is outside the 10.0.0.0/10.0.1.0 corporate ranges used for the DC (10.0.0.4) and peers (10.0.1.6), and the WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt user agents are only produced when Windows resolves a UNC/WebDAV path such as a .library-ms/.searchConnector-ms or shortcut lure. Note the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows event window (2020-05-02), so this network evidence stands on its own.

findings.title: Malicious PowerShell (steganography-decoded IEX payload) opened LSASS with full access on SCRANTON
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe PID 2976 was spawned by control.exe ("C:\Windows\System32\control.exe" /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter) at 02:58:44Z with the command line "PowerShell.exe" -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden -c "sal a New-Object;Add-Type -AssemblyName 'System.Drawing'; $g=a System.Drawing.Bitmap('C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png');...IEX([System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString(..." — a hidden, execution-policy-bypassed steganography loader reading a PNG from pbeesly's Downloads. It spawned csc.exe compiling from C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp\qkbkqqbs\qkbkqqbs.cmdline, then at 03:05:16Z opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (and winlogon.exe 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff, plus many svchost/dwm/LogonUI handles at 0x1fffff) — full-access LSASS handle acquisition consistent with credential theft / authentication-process tampering. This is the only non-system process in the dataset taking full-access handles on LSASS; the other high-access LSASS events are Microsoft-signed system binaries (wininit/csrss at boot, Azure guest-agent telemetry, AntimalwareConfig) or a wsmprovhost PowerShell-cmdlet call trace. findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 between 02:58 and 03:21 UTC, user pbeesly ran a hidden, encoded PowerShell implant on scranton.dmevals.local (PID 2976, launched by control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter, payload decoded from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png via System.Drawing and IEX). findings.title: PowerShell (pbeesly) opened a handle to lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local

The call trace resolves through ntdll/KERNELBASE and managed System.ni.dll frames ending in an UNKNOWN module, i.e. .NET code in PowerShell touching LSASS rather than a sanctioned AV/EDR component. The same user session on scranton ran an in-memory shellcode loader (VirtualAlloc/CreateThread with a 0xfc 0x48 0x83 0xe4 0xf0 byte array), a GetProcAddress/ReflectedDelegate loader with a base64 PE, and a hidden encoded PowerShell command, so the LSASS handle is consistent with credential access from that tooling. The 4663 object-access event for the same handle (scranton, pbeesly, powershell.exe, AccessMask 0x10) corroborates the LSASS touch. Other LSASS access in the window is benign: svchost.exe (289), Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe (15), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13), CollectGuestLogs.exe and MsMpEng.exe.

findings.title: Interactive pbeesly PowerShell session on SCRANTON opened LSASS with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) right after running accesschk.exe
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and 03:05:16.654Z with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff — full-access masks consistent with memory reading/dumping, not the 0x1000/0x1400 masks seen for the 289 svchost.exe and antivirus/telemetry accesses. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN modules (ntdll.dll+9c584|KERNELBASE.dll+2732e|UNKNOWN(...)), i.e. the caller was not a signed system DLL. The same session had just executed Sysinternals accesschk.exe at 03:04:34 (script block '& "C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accesschk.exe"') and exited at 03:05:08, and the host shows sdelete64.exe wiping files (C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, Draft.Zip, SysinternalsSuite.zip) and an Invoke-Exfil script block staging data to \\192.168.0.4\webdav — an active hands-on-keyboard intrusion. A matching Security 4663 object-access event on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe by C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe as pbeesly at 23:05:16 local corroborates the access. findings.title: No golden-ticket evidence: LSASS access present but no forged-TGT indicators
findings.summary: The prerequisite for a golden ticket — reading LSASS on a host holding krbtgt material — is present: PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16, and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local did the same at 03:09:29. However, no forged-ticket artefacts were observed: all 4768 events on the DC newyork.dmevals.local are for pbeesly or SCRANTON$ with PreAuthType 2 and AES256 (0x12), all 4769 requests are for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) or krbtgt, and the 4624 logons are the expected machine/system accounts plus pbeesly. No anomalous privileged account authenticated and no 4672 target-user values were returned. The LSASS access is malicious in context, but golden-ticket forging itself is not demonstrated.

findings.title: No forged web credential activity; observed credential-access precursor is LSASS access by PowerShell on SCRANTON and by wsmprovhost on NASHUA
findings.summary: No evidence of forged web credentials (no SAML/cookie/token-forgery scripting, no anomalous LogonProcessName, no SSO/ADFS endpoints in Zeek). However, the credential-access precursor is present: on scranton.dmevals.local, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and then 0x1fffff at 03:05:16.654Z, with an UNKNOWN call trace — consistent with LSASS memory access for credential material. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29.430Z, but that is explained by the pbeesly PowerShell remoting command 'Get-Process -IncludeUserName' (Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA) seen in 4104 at 23:09:23/23:09:28, i.e. benign. The same user pbeesly also ran Get-PrivateKeys (exporting cert:\LocalMachine certificates to .pfx with password 'saribas') on scranton at 23:04:56, and used PsExec (PSEXESVC.exe) against NASHUA with explicit credentials (4648). Zeek (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only internal DNS/TLS to 192.168.0.4 with no web-credential endpoints.

That agent itself was launched by services.exe and carries win.Company 'Microsoft CoreXT', i.e. it is the Azure Network Watcher VM extension, not attacker tooling. The capture was bounded: a matching 'netsh.exe trace stop' was issued by the same parent 7 seconds later (23:19:24), and only 2 netsh process creations exist in the whole sysmon window. No Npcap/WinPcap driver load (event 7), no pcap/tshark/dumpcap/windump/rawcap command line, and no capture-related service installation (7045 shows only PSEXESVC x4 and Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service) were observed. findings.title: No MFA interception activity; credential-access-adjacent hits are certificate-store reads and PsExec explicit-credential logons
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other on 2020-05-02 (02:55-03:28Z) found no MFA interception artifacts. The 16 registry hits on SmartCard/Crypto/Credential keys were all Sysmon event.code 12 (registry object access/read), not writes: SmartCardRoot certificate-store reads by powershell.exe, consent.exe, wmiprvse.exe, lsass.exe, rundll32.exe, WerFault.exe and svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, plus normal boot-time Cryptography/CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc value sets by smss.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe and taskhostw.exe. No script block referenced SmartCard, MFA, Telephony/TAPI, RADIUS/NPS, OTP, CredentialProvider, Winlogon, netsh or proxy (0 hits). The only 'token' process hit was the standard svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s TokenBroker service. The 15 event.code 4648 explicit-credential logons were PsExec service logons (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) using pbeesly's credentials on nashua.dmevals.local and scranton.dmevals.local, plus routine DWM-/UMFD-/machine-account logons from winlogon.exe, wininit.exe and taskhostw.exe. The two LogonType 10 (RDP) logons were pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 to scranton.dmevals.local with Negotiate/User32 - no smart-card or alternate MFA provider involved. findings.title: SMB share access and outbound 445 traffic are domain baseline, not forced authentication
findings.summary: The high-volume SMB hits are normal domain behaviour. All 121 event 5145 share-access events involve only the domain infrastructure shares \\*\SYSVOL (56), \\*\IPC$ (45) and \\*\ADMIN$ (20), performed by machine accounts NEWYORK$ and SCRANTON$ from the DC address 10.0.0.4 and from fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 — i.e. Group Policy/SYSVOL replication and admin-share access, not access to an attacker-controlled share. Outbound 445 Sysmon connections (66 total) go only to 10.0.0.4 (26), fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 (24) and 10.0.1.6 (16); the 10.0.1.6 connections are periodic SYSTEM/process 'System' connections repeating roughly every 60-75 seconds from scranton and nashua, consistent with DC replication. Zeek SMB connections likewise terminate on 445 (45) and 139 (5) within the internal ranges. No SMB connection to an external or unusual host was observed, so these hits do not support forced authentication.

Of 326 Sysmon event 10 accesses to lsass.exe, 289 came from C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe, 15 from the Azure IaaS Antimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe and 13 from WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe. The high-mask svchost.exe accesses (0x101001) resolve through lsm.dll, the wininit.exe/csrss.exe/services.exe accesses occur in a single burst at 03:19:09Z with call traces inside wininit.exe/basesrv.DLL/CSRSRV.dll/RPCRT4.dll, and the 0x3000 svchost access resolves through sysmain.dll — all normal OS/AV behaviour, not exploitation. The 0x1000 accesses from powershell.exe at 03:01:03Z resolve through System.ni.dll managed code (PowerShell querying process information).

No sysmon process-access (event 10) or file-create (11/23) event touched a Chrome/Firefox/Edge 'User Data' Cookies, Login Data, Web Data or Local State file, and no browser process (chrome/firefox/msedge/iexplore) appears in sysmon process creation or in any cookie-related command line. T1539 is therefore not observed; the credential-access activity on these hosts lies elsewhere.

findings.title: No domain-controller authentication backdoor observed; LSASS module loads are Microsoft-signed
findings.summary: The 33 image-load hits for lsass.exe/cryptdll.dll resolve to Microsoft-signed modules: cryptdll.dll loaded by SearchProtocolHost/SearchFilterHost/WmiPrvSE/svchost/dsregcmd/taskhostw etc. (Signature "Microsoft Windows", Signed true), and lsass.exe loading its own image plus samsrv.dll, cryptdll.dll and wdigest.dll at 03:19:09-03:19:10Z on scranton (all Microsoft-signed). No unsigned or non-System32 module was loaded into lsass.exe, and no 5136/4739 directory-service or policy-change events exist in the security log. The high-access LSASS handles from wininit.exe/csrss.exe (0x1fffff at 03:19:09Z) coincide with a boot/restart sequence on scranton, and the wsmprovhost.exe 0x1f3fff LSASS access on nashua has a call trace through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll (PowerShell cmdlet, not a credential dump). No evidence of DC authentication-process modification.

findings.title: No password-filter DLL registration found
findings.summary: Registry writes touching Control\Lsa were limited to LsaCfgFlagsDefault, LsaPid and ProductType (single writes each); no write to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Notification Packages or any Password Filter value was observed, and no new DLL was created in System32/SysWOW64. No PowerShell script block or windows.other message referenced Notification Packages or Password Filter. The only LSA-adjacent DLL loads into lsass.exe were Microsoft-signed samsrv.dll/cryptdll.dll/wdigest.dll.

findings.title: Reversible-encryption PowerShell hit is the Microsoft xActiveDirectory DSC module, not account tampering
findings.summary: The single 4104 hit matching Set-ADUser/Set-ADAccountControl/ReversibleEncryption on newyork.dmevals.local is script block cf4c3877-ec07-4e74-80b9-9258113f3933 running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM from Path C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules\xActiveDirectory\DscResources\MSFT_xADCommon\MSFT_xADCommon.ps1 — the stock Microsoft xActiveDirectory DSC helper library (Get-CommonADParameters / ConvertFrom-TimeSpan functions). It is module documentation/helper code, not a command enabling AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption. No 4739 policy-change events, no process command line with AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption, and no windows.other message mentioning Reversible exist in the data.

findings.title: No MFA/authentication policy tampering; 4670 hits are routine token permission changes
findings.summary: The security log contains no 4739 (domain policy change), 4738 (user account changed) or 5136 (directory attribute modified) events. The 143 hits for 4670 are 'Permissions on an object were changed' on Object Type: Token by machine accounts (SCRANTON$, NEWYORK$) via SearchIndexer.exe, svchost.exe and services.exe — normal service token DACL activity. The 4624 network logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25) plus pbeesly (20), with no anomalous account or MFA-bypass pattern. No evidence of MFA or authentication-policy modification.

findings.title: Hybrid-identity DLL loads are stock Microsoft cloud-auth components
findings.summary: The 18 hits for cloudap/aad/azure/ngc image loads are all Microsoft-signed (Signature "Microsoft Windows", Signed true): lsass.exe loading cloudAP.dll, aadcloudap.dll and MicrosoftAccountCloudAP.dll on scranton at 03:19:10Z, plus ngccredprov.dll/ngckeyenum.dll in LogonUI.exe, cryptngc.dll in explorer/svchost, ngcsvc.dll in svchost, and dsregcmd.exe activity. No file creation of cloudap/azuread/ngc DLLs was observed (zero hits), and no 5136/4739 directory changes exist. This is normal Windows Hello for Business / Azure AD join behaviour, not hybrid-identity backdooring.

findings.title: No network provider DLL registration or credential-provider tampering observed
findings.summary: No registry writes to NetworkProvider or credential-provider keys, no new DLL dropped into System32/SysWndrSvc paths, and no windows.other/security events referencing network provider packages were found in the retrieved data. The only credential-related activity is the malicious PowerShell LSASS access on scranton (reported under T1556) and pbeesly's PsExec-driven explicit-credential logons (4648 via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, 03:11-03:15Z), which are lateral-movement credential use rather than network-provider DLL installation.

The T1557-family checks that fired were object-access/permission events (4656/4663/4670) and generic network stacks, none of which show interception. The 4663/4656 hits on scranton.dmevals.local are pbeesly's own PowerShell/cmd/conhost accessing LSA and Winlogon registry keys during the hands-on-keyboard intrusion (e.g. C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr, powershell.exe reading \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa) — that is local credential access, not AiTM. The 4624 logons on newyork.dmevals.local are machine-account (NEWYORK$) type-3 logons from ::1/fe80::/10.0.0.4, i.e. normal DC/service traffic. Zeek (2020-04-30 window, non-overlapping with the Windows data) shows only ordinary DNS/NB name resolution and SMB mapping to 10.0.0.4 with no rogue responder or relay evidence. The real intrusion chain is: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA, then repeatedly ran .\PsExec64.exe -accepteula \\NASHUA -u "dmevals\pbeesly" -p "Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by" -i 2 "C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe", which spawned C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (parent C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) making repeated outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. Credentials were obtained by direct execution, not by poisoning/relay.
findings.title: No AiTM/relay activity observed; credential theft on scranton/nashua was direct (PowerShell + PsExec + python C2), not man-in-the-middle

findings.summary: The name-resolution and SMB checks returned only baseline traffic. Zeek DNS shows ordinary lookups (wpad.dmevals.local NXDOMAIN, wec.dmevals.local, _ldap._tcp SRV, arc.msn.com, www.bing.com) and NBNS broadcasts for SCRANTON/NASHUA to 10.0.1.255 — no rogue responder answering, no spoofed replies. SMB mapping/file records are all 10.0.1.4 / 10.0.1.6 -> 10.0.0.4 (the DC) with no relayed authentication. On the Windows side, the only service installations are PSEXESVC on nashua.dmevals.local (7045, %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, user pbeesly) and a Java VM support service on scranton — the PSEXESVC installs are the result of the attacker's own PsExec64 invocation with a plaintext password, not of a relayed SMB session. No PowerShell script block referencing LLMNR/EnableMulticast/name-resolution poisoning was found (zero hits).
findings.title: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay; SMB/NB traffic is routine and the lateral movement used explicit PsExec credentials

findings.summary: The only ARP-related activity is read-only 'arp.exe /a' execution on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:25Z, 03:19:40Z and 03:20:04Z, each spawned by Azure infrastructure agents (C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\GuestAgent\WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, WaAppAgent.exe) alongside ipconfig.exe /all, route.exe print and netsh trace start/stop. These are the standard Azure VM guest-agent/NetworkWatcher diagnostic collection sequence, run as SYSTEM, and no ARP entry modification, gratuitous ARP or duplicate-MAC behaviour was observed. No ARP-poisoning tooling or 5156/5157 UDP anomalies were found.
findings.title: ARP cache inspection on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure guest-agent diagnostics, not ARP poisoning

findings.summary: No DHCP-related events were found: the DHCP client/server operational checks (1341/1342/1020/1063) returned zero hits in windows.other, and no UDP 5156/5157 network events indicative of DHCP spoofing appeared in windows.security. Zeek shows only normal broadcast traffic (NBNS to 10.0.1.255, NetBIOS datagram to 10.0.1.255:138) and no rogue DHCP OFFER/ACK. findings.title: No DHCP spoofing or rogue DHCP server activity observed
No silver-ticket evidence: no forged service tickets or anomalous service-account logons
findings.summary: All 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local in the window are for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with AES256 encryption (0x12) and status 0x0, originating from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6. No service account (e.g. a user SPN account) requested tickets, and no 4672 special-privilege logon target users were returned. The 4634 logoff distribution is 227 type-3 and 9 type-2, consistent with normal network/interactive sessions. The LSASS reads by PowerShell/wsmprovhost are malicious credential access but there is no evidence of forged service tickets being used.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS requests or service-account ticket bursts
findings.summary: Kerberoasting would appear as a burst of 4769 requests for user/service SPNs with RC4 (0x17) encryption. In this window the DC newyork.dmevals.local logged only 4769 requests for machine accounts and krbtgt, all AES256 (0x12), and the zeek kerberos log (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) shows 14 AS and 11 TGS requests, all for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL against krbtgt, cifs/NEWYORK, cifs/NASHUA, ldap/NEWYORK.dmevals.local and HTTP/NASHUA with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96. No roasting tooling (Rubeus, GetUserSPNs, Invoke-Kerberoast) appeared in process creation or PowerShell script blocks. The LSASS access on SCRANTON/NASHUA is malicious but is not Kerberoasting.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting: all AS-REQs pre-authenticated, no roasting tooling
findings.summary: AS-REP roasting requires AS-REQs for accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication. Every 4768 in the window (for pbeesly and SCRANTON$) carries PreAuthType 2, i.e. pre-authentication was performed, and the zeek kerberos log shows the expected KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by a successful pre-authenticated AS exchange for pbeesly/DMEVALS.LOCAL. No Rubeus/GetNPUsers/ASREP activity was found in process creation or PowerShell script blocks (the dedicated ES|QL checks returned zero rows).

findings.title: No web cookie theft or forgery observed
findings.summary: The cookie-focused check (4663 on *Cookies*) returned zero hits, and no PowerShell script block referenced cookies, SAML, ADFS, AADSSO, token duplication or impersonation (4104 search returned 0). The only web traffic in the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows data) is internal DNS lookups (newyork.dmevals.local, wpad.dmevals.local, wec.dmevals.local, _ldap._tcp.pdc._msdcs.dmevals.local) and TLS to 192.168.0.4 with a single internal issuer; the two HTTP requests are from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4. Nothing indicates cookie theft or forged session cookies.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery observed; logon activity is normal Kerberos/Advapi plus PsExec and RDP by pbeesly
findings.summary: Successful logons (4624) are dominated by machine accounts and SYSTEM with LogonProcessName Kerberos (217) and Advapi (76); the rare values are a single NtLmSsp NTLM network logon (type 3) and two User32 type-10 logons for pbeesly from 172.18.39.2 on scranton.dmevals.local at 23:20:41-23:20:46, plus one '-' type-0 SYSTEM entry — consistent with normal RDP/console logon, not forged SAML assertions. Explicit-credential logons (4648) are pbeesly to NASHUA (10.0.1.6) and PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, plus standard DWM/UMFD/winlogon/taskhostw entries. No SAML/ADFS/AADSSO artifacts appear in PowerShell script blocks or file access events.

findings.title: No MFA request generation observed; hosts show credential theft, lateral movement and archive collection instead
findings.summary: Hunted all four Windows datasets (2020-05-02 02:55Z-03:28Z) for T1621 (Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation). No MFA/authenticator/OTP/verification-prompt tooling or artifacts were found: a sysmon process-creation sweep for mfa/auth/otp/token/push/login/azure/dsregcmd command lines returned only benign Azure guest-agent and OS components (dsregcmd.exe launched by svchost -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule, TokenBroker/PushToInstall svchost services, CollectGuestLogs.exe, logman.exe, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe); a message-text sweep of windows.other for mfa/multi-factor/authenticator/one-time/verification code/phonefactor returned 0 rows; and the security log shows no failed-logon (4625) or NTLM (4776) burst that would accompany prompt bombing - only a single 4776 for pbeesly from workstation 10.0.1.4. The only interactive logons are two LogonType 10 (User32) events for pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local from 172.18.39.2. The real attacker activity in this window is credential access and lateral movement, not MFA abuse: on scranton.dmevals.local user pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe from PowerShell four times with the plaintext password of dmevals\pbeesly to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on NASHUA (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42), each producing a 4648 explicit-credential logon on scranton (source 10.0.1.6) and nashua; on NASHUA the python.exe spawned powershell.exe and cmd.exe, ran a recursive file-collection script (ChildItem over *.doc/*.xls/*.pdf/*.zip/*pst/*psw*/*pass*/*login*/*vpn etc. into $env:APPDATA\working.zip) and staged it with .\Rar.exe a -hpfGzq5yKw to Desktop\working.zip; on scranton pbeesly also ran sdelete64.exe against C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip. None of this constitutes MFA request generation.

findings.title: Benign certificate-store registry write and Kerberos TGT requests
findings.summary: The 4657 on nashua is a SYSTEM Sysmon.exe write of an unreadable Blob under SystemCertificates\ROOT, and the 4768s on newyork are normal AES256 preauth krbtgt TGTs.

incidents.title: PowerShell shellcode loader and full-access LSASS handles on SCRANTON/NASHUA

LSASS memory access is best characterized as OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory.

incidents.title: DS-Replication-Get-Changes access on NEWYORK by machine account
incidents.rationale: A 4662 event shows DS-Replication-Get-Changes GUID access, the DCSync right, though by the host's own machine account on itself, so low confidence.

incidents.title: WebDAV forced-authentication from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: DavClnt/WebDAV-MiniRedir OPTIONS/PROPFIND sequence with 401 then 207 shows the classic forced-authentication handshake to capture credentials.

incidents.rationale: Explorer Recent .lnk files and a PowerShell-written StartUp hostui.lnk were created; the finding itself notes the StartUp .lnk is persistence rather than forced auth, but the lure-style shortcuts are best mapped to forced authentication among in-scope techniques.

incidents.rationale: Under pbeesly, PowerShell on scranton and nashua enumerated user profiles for *pass*/*login*/*vpn* and document files and compressed them (Compress-Archive, Rar.exe with password, sdelete64 wipe). This is harvesting credentials stored in files.

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil staging and WebDAV exfiltration with embedded credentials
incidents.rationale: Both describe the Invoke-Exfil scriptblock (psversion.ps1) compressing Downloads into a password-protected 7z and copying to \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd! credentials. The credential-access element is plaintext credentials embedded in scripts.

incidents.title: PsExec64 from SCRANTON passing cleartext domain password to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: PsExec64 invoked with -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by to launch python.exe on \\NASHUA, producing PSEXESVC logons. The credential-access aspect is a cleartext password in a command line.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys certificate export to .pfx with hardcoded password on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same Get-PrivateKeys scriptblock (readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and exporting certificates to .pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas', producing coyn5igj.3io.pfx. This is theft of private keys.

incidents.title: Unsigned hostui.exe launched elevated from PowerShell on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: PowerShell ran Start-Process hostui.exe -verb runas; the unsigned, metadata-less binary at High integrity is consistent with a credential-theft helper accessing Windows Credential Manager.

incidents.title: No golden-ticket evidence despite LSASS access
incidents.rationale: LSASS access prerequisite present but no forged-TGT artifacts; mapped to Golden Ticket as the closest in-scope technique for the assessed hypothesis.

incidents.title: Hidden steganography-decoded PowerShell implant (monkey.png) launched via control.exe on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter spawned hidden, execution-policy-bypassed PowerShell that decoded a payload from monkey.png and IEX'd it. This is obfuscated execution, not credential access.

incidents.title: Malicious .scr dropper in C:\ProgramData\victim executed by pbeesly on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same event: explorer.exe launching C:\ProgramData\victim\<odd-name>cod.3aka3.scr with /S as pbeesly, spawning cmd.exe/conhost and later wiped with sdelete64. This is user execution of a malicious file, not credential access.

context_out_of_scope.title: csc.exe compiles attacker C# from temp cmdline files on SCRANTON
context_out_of_scope.summary: pbeesly's hidden PowerShell invoked csc.exe twice with @qkbkqqbs.cmdline / @0piklvia.cmdline, producing qkbkqqbs.dll and 0piklvia.dll in AppData\Local\Temp.

context_out_of_scope.title: sdclt.exe launched three times by cmd.exe on SCRANTON
context_out_of_scope.summary: cmd.exe started sdclt.exe three times at 02:58:42-43, immediately before the csc.exe compilation and Explorer Recent .lnk writes; sdclt is a known UAC-bypass/backup-abuse binary.
